Children of a Dead Earth is one of the most technically ambitious space strategy games ever made, and it immediately becomes clear that the game was designed for players who are deeply interested in realistic physics, orbital mechanics, engineering, and hard science fiction. Unlike most space combat games that rely on cinematic explosions, arcade-style dogfights, and simplified systems, this game treats space warfare with near-obsessive realism. Every ship movement, weapon system, heat signature, and orbital maneuver is governed by believable scientific principles. The result is less like a traditional video game and more like a complex military simulation exploring what actual combat in space could realistically look like in the distant future.

The setting establishes a bleak vision of humanity after the destruction of Earth. Civilization has spread across the solar system, where isolated factions now compete over resources, territory, and survival. While the narrative itself remains fairly minimal, the atmosphere created by the worldbuilding is extremely effective. Space feels cold, hostile, and militarized, with every conflict carrying a sense of desperation rather than heroism. The game avoids flashy science-fiction fantasy and instead presents a future where technology still obeys harsh physical limitations. This grounded approach gives the entire experience a very distinctive tone compared to more traditional sci-fi strategy games.

What truly separates Children of a Dead Earth from nearly every other space combat title is its dedication to realism. Ships are not agile starfighters making impossible turns or firing endless energy weapons without consequence. They are fragile machines built around realistic propulsion systems, fuel limitations, thermal management, and vulnerable internal components. Weapons such as railguns, lasers, missiles, and nuclear devices behave according to believable scientific rules. Lasers generate massive heat, projectiles require predictive calculations over huge distances, and missiles must deal with realistic acceleration and interception problems. Even something as simple as radiator placement or reactor output can determine whether a ship survives battle or destroys itself through overheating.

Ship construction becomes one of the most rewarding and intellectually engaging parts of the game. Players can design spacecraft almost entirely from scratch by selecting engines, reactors, radiators, armor thickness, fuel storage, weapons, ammunition types, and support systems. Every design decision has advantages and drawbacks. Heavier armor increases survivability but reduces maneuverability and acceleration. More powerful engines improve tactical flexibility but create enormous heat-management problems. Weapon choices drastically affect engagement ranges and combat doctrine. Designing ships feels closer to aerospace engineering than traditional game customization, and players who enjoy experimentation and optimization will likely become completely absorbed by the possibilities.

Combat itself is unlike almost any other strategy game. Battles unfold slowly and methodically, often beginning long before ships are even within visible range of each other. Orbital positioning, intercept calculations, fuel reserves, and detection systems all matter before the first shot is fired. Once combat begins, players must manage weapon firing solutions, acceleration vectors, heat buildup, ammunition conservation, and defensive positioning simultaneously. The game uses a hybrid pause-and-command system that allows players to carefully analyze situations while still maintaining tension during engagements. Victories feel genuinely satisfying because success comes from planning, engineering, and tactical foresight rather than quick reflexes.

One of the game’s most fascinating achievements is how effectively it communicates the terrifying reality of realistic space warfare. Ships are incredibly fragile, and a single successful strike can cripple engines, destroy reactors, or kill entire crews instantly. Battles are often decided by detection ranges, maneuver planning, and resource management rather than dramatic exchanges of fire. Heat becomes just as dangerous as enemy weapons because managing thermal buildup is essential for keeping systems operational. The game constantly reinforces the idea that space combat would likely be brutally unforgiving and heavily dependent on physics rather than cinematic heroics.

The atmosphere is strengthened further by the audio design and presentation style. Music remains subtle and restrained, creating a cold and isolated mood rather than relying on dramatic orchestral themes. Sound effects are minimal but effective, helping reinforce the sterile and mechanical nature of the setting. The lack of exaggerated spectacle actually works in the game’s favor because it keeps the focus entirely on tension, calculation, and realism. Combined with the scientific approach to gameplay, the atmosphere becomes uniquely immersive for players interested in hard science fiction.

However, the same realism that makes the game fascinating also creates its biggest weakness. Children of a Dead Earth has an extremely steep learning curve that can easily overwhelm new players. Understanding orbital mechanics, propulsion systems, thermal control, targeting solutions, and realistic combat strategies requires patience and genuine interest in the science behind the systems. Tutorials exist, but the game still expects players to invest significant time learning its mechanics. Players looking for accessible strategy gameplay or fast-paced action will likely struggle during the early hours.

The interface can also feel intimidating and overly technical. Menus are filled with engineering data, numerical readouts, and detailed ship statistics that often resemble professional simulation software more than a traditional game interface. Battles can occasionally become difficult to visually interpret because so much of the complexity happens beneath the surface through calculations and invisible systems. Some players may appreciate this depth, while others may feel disconnected from the action because the simulation prioritizes realism over spectacle.

Pacing will also divide players heavily. Combat is slow, deliberate, and heavily focused on preparation. Long stretches of planning and maneuvering are common, which may feel exhausting for players expecting constant action or cinematic battles. The game intentionally sacrifices excitement for authenticity, and that design choice will not appeal to everyone.

Despite these flaws, Children of a Dead Earth succeeds because of how completely committed it is to its vision. It refuses to simplify its systems into conventional arcade mechanics and instead delivers one of the most scientifically grounded portrayals of space warfare ever attempted in gaming. Very few games are willing to embrace realism this deeply, and the result is a genuinely unique experience.

For players fascinated by hard science fiction, realistic military simulations, and highly technical strategy games, Children of a Dead Earth offers an experience unlike almost anything else available. It is difficult, demanding, and occasionally overwhelming, but beneath the intimidating complexity lies one of the most intellectually rewarding space combat simulations ever created.

Several clones of the hard-scifi space combat simulator are coming out now (and, chances are, I will buy several of them), with thermonuclear engines, Delta-V management, and radiators, but this is, as far as I can tell, the father of them all. I played this when it first came out, and it completely changed the way I view the prospect of warfare in space.

While the game does a better job than any other I've played at simulating realistic space combat it fails horrifically as an actual game. It crashes at a frequency well in excess of what could be considered reasonable which if it happens during a lengthy mission means restarting from the beginning. If you or the enemy are using more than a few projectiles, which is the case for the enemy in nearly all campaign missions, then the frame rate will suffer severely and the odds of a crash rises substantially. Finally, if the ai attempts any kind of maneuver you must then make a counter maneuver meaning that you will often spend 30+ minutes during the campaign making micro adjustments to try and get an intercept to actually stick, spend upwards of an hour waiting through 0 threat battles with drone or missile swarms that any competent player ship can obliterate from well outside enemy range, only to have the game crash before the mission can be completed. Give me a version of this game where you can auto maintain reasonable intercepts, combat can be fast forwarded, and I can expect to play an entire mission without a crash and I'd be able to give it a glowing recommendation, this is not that game.

I finally started playing this game after months of it sitting and intimidating me!  First off - it looks scary.  Kerbal Space Program was already a huge time sink and about as complex as I wanted to have to deal with, and then this comes along and I think "hmmm... looks too hard!"

But the feature that differentiates Children of a Dead Earth from KSP, and what actually makes it EASIER to play, is time pausing.  KSP doesn't let you pause at all, which is not a big deal in reality (most of the time) but sometimes, when your ship is about to burn up and you're FRANTICALLY trying to keep spinning it just to stay alive... well it gets really freaking intense and there's no pause button other than bringing up the game save menu.  But for Children of a Dead Earth, it's almost a turn-based strategy game, where the game automatically pauses, you enter in your next move, and then you tell it to go forward by whatever time increment you selected, which can be 1 minute, 10 minutes, 1 hour, etc.  This really dropped my anxiety while playing this, and I think it makes the game much more accessible.

I have only played the first mission - but once I saw how the time freezing works I thought "well this is brilliant!  I never would have thought of that!!" and I'm sold on the concept.  If I see more stuff to write about I will, but generally if you like KSP or even if you're new to orbital mechanics and want to learn, this is a great introduction!

This is one of the most unusual space games I’ve ever come across. The idea of an ultra-realistic space combat simulator, based on real orbital mechanics, physics, and engineering, is thrilling in itself. Every ship, rocket, and drone requires precise calculations- Δv, speed, trajectory, the gravitational influence of all celestial bodies - you have to account for all of it to complete a mission successfully. There’s almost no freedom in the game. Every mission turns into a true engineering puzzle, where you must perform the one correct action at the exact right moment, or the outcome will be a failure. Ship design only becomes available after completing a particularly difficult mission, and that’s when the game truly reveals its full potential.

This game is absolutely unique. There's quite literally nothing like it that I know of unless you want to rip your hair out modding Kerbal Space Program, and even then you won't be able to dive into module design anywhere near as much as you can in this game.

I should first note a few cons, mainly that the AI in general isn't very smart at all at range and the controls for making maneuvers and intercepts in the map view can be quite finnicky and hard to get just right. The combat is also instanced. Because of this there can be times when enemies launch flak missiles at your incoming missile barrage and the ship they came from that's only 25km away won't show up in the instance, for example. I think if a sequel or spiritual successor to this game is ever made, it needs to be much more seamless and have more refined maneuver controls. Additionally I do also disagree with the use of the AI-generated portrait in the store image. I think the plain art with no face and just the title, like the banner you see in your library, looks much better on its own.

Much better than all of that though is basically everything related to the actual engineering and direct combat side of this game, including the sandbox mode. It's far from perfect but I have easily spent most of my time in this game designing ships and crazy weapons or missiles and having them just go at each other with the instant action mode. I do also find the lore and setting to be quite cool, even if it's not the most realistic.

Even with the limitations and imperfections of the design tools you can do some fun things. Do you want to make 1kg micro-nukes with a 99t yield launched from cannons at 7km/s? One giant ship-sized missile with highly efficient armor that detonates 30Mt of nukes at once and deletes anything nearby and is super hard to destroy? This game lets you. It feels like a lot of the stock modules and ships included are deliberately designed to be subpar to encourage you to make better versions of them. Also if you have photosensitive epilepsy (or just find flashing annoying) and want to play with nukes I HIGHLY recommend you turn off the bloom in the video settings so your whole screen doesn't light up 3 times per second.

The music by Nigel Stanford is also something I can't neglect to mention because I feel like it was an absolutely perfect choice for this game's atmosphere and theme of juxtaposing high-energy orbital combat with the slow dancing of celestial motion. The guitar that kicks in during the track "Deep Space Cut" is unforgettable the first time you hear it.

I enthusiastically recommend this game to anyone who is interested in hard sci-fi space combat and has a familiarity with orbital mechanics. As of the writing of this review, you're not going to find a game that depicts the chaotic beauty of point defense cannons, turreted lasers and high-velocity railgun broadsides as well as CoaDE does.

I think a good way to describe this game is being extremely book smart rather than street smart. Sounds dumb but hear me out.

Overall the physics in the game is very realistic and the customization is in depth. You can create your own engines, reactors, weapons and armor all based on real physics and material science stock in game, and build a ship from this that will fly like a real spacecraft. The use of n-body physics rather than a more simple system, like KSP uses adds to this. At the time I'm writing this I've probably spent more time building and editing spaceships rather than playing the actual game; it's that in depth. There's a lot of stuff in the game that I haven't touched because you'd probably need some kind of degree to understand what's going on, like the nuclear reactors. Now that's the book smart side of the game, which frankly it excels at. The street smart part is where it all starts to fall apart.

First of all, the AI is this game is dumb. REALLY dumb. Formations made up of dozens of drones will spend all their deltaV chasing after a passerby with it's engine turned off or a ship that has already been defeated, and friendly ships will make unnecessarily aggressive maneuvers if they get too close to any of their comrades, sending them spinning into the void. Speaking of ship AI, the ship AI, or the captain you could call it, for whatever reason is overwhelmed by the ability to bank the craft and if given the ability to do so will send the craft into a spin so monstrously violent that the whole crew will be turned to mush. Legit I added a gimbal unit to the retro thrusters on a ship I made to help with turning the ship into the correct orientation when broadside, and my ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ down syndrome pilot would kill everyone on board by rotating the ship in such a fashion not dissimilar to how you'd expect a dreidel to spin when chucked into the air and drop kicked across your  living room. I was confused by this phenomena and thought that the enemy must have some type of railgun that would hit my ship so hard it'd incapacitate the whole crew via the g forces, but alas such a weapon didn't exist.

There's also a lot of small details in the game that detract from the realism and made me smh. For example, why are space missiles hundreds of years in the future still relying on the method of heat seeking? I'd understand it if these missiles were used in close quarters but these missiles have a theoretical range of thousands, if not hundreds of thousands of kilometers. Where's the radar?? The missiles being IR also makes them essentially useless as they can be defeated with a few flares and deactivated engines, which is just silly. Going back to the retro thrusters of the previous paragraph, where are the bundled RCS units? Retro thusters in this game are represented by large, singular engines when in real life they are made up of multiple smaller ones which can propel the craft in all axis in both rotation and translation.

This is more of a personal gripe rather than an objective flaw in the game but I still think it's worth pointing out. For a setting set hundreds, possibly one or two thousand years in the future based on the lore snippets we get throughout the game, the engine tech is pretty lame. Like you expect me to believe that in a world where humanity has colonized the entire solar system, including the outer planets, that we'd still be limited to nuclear thermal engines as the ideal method of propulsion? No nuclear salt rockets, no fusion or orion drives, no nothing? I don't know I just wish the game had some more ambition.

Overall the science in the game is cool and it's a nice game for the more nerdy type of player, but a lot of the systems in the game start to break and/or fail when you try to do stuff that's more outside the box; reminds me of space engineers. (also if anyone does read this so many years after the game's release, please don't take any of the language too seriously. I've noticed my writing style can be a little dramatic at times and if it comes across as ranty or whiny that wasn't my intention.
